replying_to: Replying to Faster and Smarter AutoAugment: Augmentation Policy Search Based on Dynamic Data-Clustering
display_title: Interesting, but the details are missing

content.title: Interesting, but the details are missing
content.review:
## Summary of this paper

This paper introduces Faster and Smarter AutoAugment (FSAA). FASS is a variant of AutoAugment and searches for data augmentation policies using Bayesian optimization with data clustering. FSAA improves the performance of image classification models and the robustness for adversarial attacks.

## Strengths
* FSAA finds data augmentation policies almost as fast as DADA, which is a differentiable AutoAugment variant.
* The authors extensively conducted experiments on various datasets.

## Weaknesses

* Data split is an essential factor of this paper, but only the protocol to split is explained. Why this method works and accelerates searching should be included. Except for this data split, FSAA is almost eqaul to FAA.
* The reason that FSAA is almost as fast as DADA is not described. Gradient-based optimization is usually more efficient than black-box optimization, and why 
* Neither tables nor figures show standard deviations. I know writing standard deviations in the tables is difficult in the limited space, but they can be easily included in figures.
* Improvement of robustness is a side-effect. Then, are there any interpretations why FSAA shows better robustness than FAA?

## Questions

> to apply the differentiable methodology, the surface of the objective function for the augmentation policy must be assumed to be a convex shape (page 3)
* I don't think both Faster AutoAugment [Hataya+20] and DADA [Li+20] assume the loss functions of policies are convex. As far as I know, SGD methods work even if loss functions are nonconvex. The orignal loss space that FSAA uses seems also nonconvex.

## Recommendation

* OK, but not good enough. This method shows good performance. However, the details are missing, and the novelty from Fast AutoAugment [Lim+2019] is limited. See Weakness for more details.

## Comments

* Yin+19 reported that AutoAugment improves CNNs' robustness.

Yin et al. A Fourier Perspective on Model Robustness in Computer Vision. NeurIPS 2019.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

display_title: A fast learned augmentation technique - but it fails to cite and compare against RandAugment

content.title: A fast learned augmentation technique - but it fails to cite and compare against RandAugment
content.review:
There is unfortunately a major issue with this paper - it doesn't cite or compare against RandAugment, and it is a big deal.
This paper is about improving AutoAugment (AA) by Cubuk et al. AA was followed by Faster AutoAugment (FAA) by Hataya et al. and this work (FSAA) is about improving the search speed of FAA and therefore mainly compares itself against FAA. FAA is faster than AA, but is not more accurate. However, the original authors of AA - Cubuk et al. - released another paper called RandAugment (RA) last year after FAA, and showed that an extremely simplistic uniform sampling method that can be implemented in 10 lines of code performed better than AA (and therefore better than FAA), without searching for data augmentation policies. It also showed that learned augmentation methods such as AA or PBA suffered from systematic drawbacks. In essence, RA proved that AA was a faulty approach. Therefore it is a big deal that this paper fails to cite and compare against the RA paper. The full reference is:

"RandAugment: Practical automated data augmentation with a reduced search space", Cubuk et al.

I don't think a paper on learned augmentation can be accepted at a top conference right now without comparing itself against RA . Even though the proposed method claims to be 10x-20x faster than FAA, it doesn't change the fact that RA is essentially search-free and performs even better than AA. This paper reports slightly better results than FAA, but it's not clear how it compares against AA, and more importantly to RA, which is already more accurate than AA.

The authors should i) discuss the systematic drawbacks of learned augmentation as shown by the RA paper and prove that their method is less prone (if it is), ii) implement and compare against RA in terms of accuracy. If the paper can claim (significantly) higher accuracy than RA, then it has merit. Without doing this, I don't think that it can be accepted.

The paper itself is written clearly and shows very clear improvements over FAA by a clever data clustering scheme when selecting policies, which leads to 10x-20x improvement in speed, as well as gains in accuracy compared to FAA. The method is also compared against differentiable automatic data augmentation (DADA), and is shown to be almost as fast but also slightly more accurate. The experimental results are persuasive and the analyses are satisfactory. The main issue I can find with the paper is what's described above, which unfortunately means that the paper should be rejected in its current state.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

display_title: Some impressive results, but I have concerns about evaluation and presentation

content.title: Some impressive results, but I have concerns about evaluation and presentation
content.review:
This paper presents a new way of searching for data augmentation strategies that is claimed to be more efficient and accurate. The method is evaluated on 4 different datasets (CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, and SVHN) and 2-3 different architectures on each dataset. The authors' proposed method, FSAA, outperforms the included baselines on about half of the {architecture, dataset} pairs on clean accuracy. The authors also evaluate 3 different aspects of the robustness of their models (FGSM accuracy, center occlusion, and boundary occlusion) relative to 2 other chosen augmentation methods.

The paper has impressive results on some of the models they evaluate on, and I appreciate that they also evaluate the robustness of their models in addition to clean accuracy. However, I do not believe the method is a sufficient improvement over previous methods, and I find the number of tasks included in the paper insufficient. I am also unsure about why some baselines were included for comparisons and while some were not. Because of these reasons, I do not believe the current draft should be accepted. I detail below my concerns as well as some my minor comments. I would be very happy to update my score if the authors can address my concerns.  

1) I am curious about why the authors chose to include some of the existing augmentation strategies for comparison but not others. For example, Adversarial AutoAugment paper has reported accuracies that outperform FSAA on some of the benchmarks presented in the paper. Similarly, AutoAugment and RandAugment's reported results are better than FSAA on some of the models, and RandAugment does not even have a separate search phase on a proxy task. PBA has achieved low search cost for cifar datasets, and would be an important comparison to include in Table 2. If the authors only want to compare to methods whose code or policies are opensourced, AutoAugment, RandAugment, and PBA would all fall under this category. 

2) The authors only evaluate on a single task which is classification, and only on datasets that have been studied extensively using the same augmentation operations from PIL. As far as I can tell, the only transfer experiment the authors have done is between cifar-10 and cifar-100, which are hardly different enough to be considered a transfer. Even the early paper of AutoAugment had tried transferring from ImageNet to several FGVC datasets. Similarly, why not include more challenging tasks and datasets that can showcase the advantages of the proposed method. For example, CutMix had included a weakly-supervised localization task, and finetuned on Pascal detection and COCO image captioning tasks. RandAugment had evaluated their method on object detection as well. Since even simple methods such as CutMix and RandAugment can do well on these classification tasks, it might be useful to the community if newly proposed augmentation strategies evaluated on more challenging tasks. 

3) I am surprised that CutMix seems to not do very well in the authors' evaluations on several small datasets, and even lower the accuracy by 1.4% on RXN trained on ImageNet. CutMix does not have any hyperparameters to tune, but is it possible that better results could be achieved by tuning learning rate, weight decay, or some other regularization options on this baseline? I am not very familiar with the RXN model, however knowing how well CutMix does on other models, I find it surprising that it would lower the accuracy here. Do the authors know why this might be happening for this specific baseline? 

4) Could the authors comment on the novelty of their approach, especially relative to Fast AutoAugment and CTAugment from the FixMatch paper? As far as I know, both of these papers also used the accuracy of a base model on augmented data as their main method of inferring the efficacy of an augmentation policy, and Fast AutoAugment also used Bayesian optimization to update the policies.  Given these, the current paper does not seem too different to me, in terms of its general approach, from the Fast AutoAugment method. Furthermore, their results do not seem to be much better than Fast AutoAugment either, except perhaps for the RXN model on ImageNet. 

Minor comments:

1) I think that the authors do not need 2 decimal figures for their reported errors on the small datasets. Although the standard deviation of their runs is not reported, it is generally on the order of 0.1%-0.2%, which implies that the second decimal point reported for accuracy is not informative. Furthermore, the authors used only one decimal point for accuracy on ImageNet, which should arguably use more decimals than the small datasets since it has a larger validation set and the fluctuations due to random initializations are smaller. 

2) While I appreciate that the authors also evaluated the robustness of their models, I am not sure how much I learned from these measurements. It seems like CM, FAA, and FSAA all do about the same on FGSM, and the no-augmentation model is much worse. This is probably mainly due to the clean accuracy increase from any advanced augmentation. I also find FGSM to be not as useful a distortion, since it can easily be subject to gradient obfuscation. I would suggest evaluating the robustness under Gaussian noise, which does not have this problem and is more generally relevant to other kinds of robustness.  I do find it interesting that while CutMix does much better on clean accuracy on ResNet-50, it seems to do worse on occlusion robustness benchmarks. It might be interesting to compare to RandAugment here, as it is likely to have better robustness on these benchmarks compared to FAA due to higher diversity. 

3) I do not think the authors need to call their method "smarter" -- their method is certainly faster, which is an objective, measurable quantity. I would suggest using a more precise and objective terminology. 

4) In the first sentence of introduction, I do not understand how data augmentation is a "normalization" technique. Did the authors mean it is a "regularization technique"?
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review:
The paper proposes yet another variant of the Fast Auto-Augment type of augmentation policy search. At search time the data is repeatedly split according to the current augmentation policies. The data splitting and the augmentation policy search are both using Bayesian optimization with ("loss" - "top-1 accuracy") objective. Comparable or better performance (to naive baseline, FAA, CutMix, DADA)  is reported on a range of models and datasets (including CIFAR-10/100, SCHN, and ImageNet).  Though gains do not seem great.

Pros:
- AutoML is the way future models would eventually all train and auto-augmentation is a big chunk of that, hence the paper deals with an important topic.
- Some gains are observed, especially for smaller models, and 0.8% / 0.5% on ImageNet w.r.t. FAA on a very recent RexNet model on ImageNet
- automatic data clustering during policy search seems the right way to go (yet I think similar to what FAA also does)
- the speed of the proposed method seems to be better than the competition, except DADA.

Cons:
- the writing could be improved, many details that would allow some form of a reproduction attempt seem to be missing, and overall the methods applied at different stages are not 100% clear (small example, it seems at test time the policy is being used with linearly changing probabilities that eventually get inverted???). As code was not included, and no promise of releasing it was made, I feel this paper might be not useful for the readers if they would like to build upon it in their future AA research.
- the main gains are demonstrated either on the smaller WRN models, or on the very recent RexXNet model (good, yet not super fair), my expectation was to see significant improvement on the SS models, yet there it is only comparable.
- the authors complain about other methods, such as DADA, not taking sufficient care to avoid local optima, yet the intuition behind their own method is hardly explained, and only empirical arguments are provided. Overall, I would suggest both explaining what they are doing in a clearer form, but also provide better intuition for their methods and choices.

To summarize: 
the proposed method seems to show some benefits in terms of speed and comparable accuracy of found AA policy, yet in my view needs to be significantly improved in terms of clarity, intuition, and reproducibility to be useful to the ICLR audience. I urge the authors to improve upon these points, and will monitor other reviewers opinions and author's rebuttal to further verify the validity of my concerns or their potential resolution.
content.confidence: 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct
